article_text:
プッチーニの傑作、オペラの中のオペラ

政情不安に揺れるローマを舞台に、運命に翻弄される歌姫トスカと共和派の画家カヴァラドッシの愛と悲劇を、プッチーニが甘美な旋律と劇的なオーケストラで描いた傑作オペラです。

ナポレオン軍がオーストリア軍に勝利した歴史的な 1 日を切り取った緊迫のドラマ、そして美しくドラマティックな“声のエンターテインメント”たるオペラの魅力を存分に楽しめる、オペラの中のオペラです。

豪華なキャストで名アリアを存分に

指揮にはイタリア・オペラの巨匠ドナート・レンツェッティ、注目のトスカはオペラ界のスターとして輝くソプラノ、カルメン・ジャンナッタージョ、カヴァラドッシにはベルカントからドラマティックな役柄へとスケールを増すトップ・テノール、サイミール・ピルグ、スカルピアは世界屈指の人気バリトン、ダリボール・イェニスが出演。オペラファンには見逃せない上演です。

＜あらすじ＞ 1800 年6月、オーストリア支配下のローマ。共和派の画家カヴァラドッシは、脱獄した友人アンジェロッティを匿った罪で捕らえられる。トスカをわがものにしようと狙う警視総監スカルピアは、トスカの面前で恋人カヴァラドッシを拷問し、命を救う代償にトスカ自身を要求。取引に応じたトスカは、カヴァラドッシを形だけの死刑とする約束を取り付け、出国許可証を手にするが、偶然手にし たナイフでスカルピアを刺し殺す。明け方、見せかけのはずの銃殺刑が行われるが…。

article_text:
October began with Ben Affleck and Kerry Washington premiering “Animals,” their new political thriller about a Los Angeles mayoral candidate (Affleck) whose family is thrust into an unimaginable situation involving their son and housekeeper and her undocumented immigrant boyfriend.

The following day, the Critics Choice Association hosted its sixth annual Celebración of Cinema & Television in Beverly Hills. John Leguizamo delivered a tear-filled acceptance speech when he was presented with the Career Achievement Award.

In New York City, Pedro Pascal walked the red carpet at the New York Film Festival for the world premiere of his Tony Gilroy -directed drama “Behemoth!”

Take a look at the best red carpet and event photos so far from October 2026 below. Keep checking back all month long for more.

article_text:
Three films into its latest “chapter” (this one subtitled “Gods and Monsters”), James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DCU can’t be faulted for making interesting choices. Hell, at least they’re making choices at all. Kicking off their incarnation of the latest run of comic book movies with “Superman” was unquestionably smart (it’s Superman! you know him!), even if its follow-up “Supergirl” was destined to divide audiences (even if this critic quite liked it, surely there are other reasons why some members of this seemingly dedicated audience didn’t, no matter its quality).

Enter: “Clayface.” Another set of execs and filmmakers wouldn’t have bellied up to this grim, gross anti-hero to round out their first trio of movies meant to reset a massive franchise. But does that kind of ambition and vision pay off in James Watkins ‘ goopy, gory, decidedly R-rated body horror feature? Not so much, even as open-minded audiences will likely admire the big swings on offer here. It’s certainly different , and for comic book movie fans absolutely bored to death by the same old stuff , it’s something of a respite. Yet, divorced from all that, Watkins’ film confounds much more than it compels.

A working knowledge of Clayface lore is not required to understand the film — the script from Mike Flangan and Hossein Amini lays out the essentials with ease, before collapsing in the film’s second half — though it’s perhaps helpful to know that that he’s always been imagined as a Batman adversary . Fair enough. Those bones of the story (bones! those will soon be in short supply!) hint at perhaps why he was chosen for this early story in the new DCU : get some Batman winks in there, introduce us to Gotham City, toy with some dark underbelly stuff.

Flanagan and Amini also latch on to another bit of early Clayface backstory: he’s an actor, a pretty natty way to make horrific facial scarring really hurt. Matt Hagen ( Tom Rhys Harries , very good at conveying genuine pathos under gobs of makeup and VFX) is a Gotham City native, a wrong-side-of-the-tracks kid who is on the cusp of superstardom. When we first meet him, he’s about to be nominated for a major award (on-screen graphics don’t say what it is, though someone later calls it an Academy Award, sure ), fielding great new offers, and trying to stay grounded. His best pal Corey (Joshua James) helps, as do his frequent mentions of his fraught early life.

Matt is, by all accounts, a nice guy. He introduces himself to the pretty flight attendant on the private jet! He’s sweet to his agent! He goes back home to Gotham to chat with other rising young performers! But Matt is also — and this is something the film can never quite square — a bit too easily swayed by a pretty face and a night out at the club. When an alluring young lady (Joana Ribeiro) makes eyes at him across the dance floor, he can’t resist (even when she tells him she’s an aspiring actor; run, dude!). Thank goodness Corey is on hand to remind Matt that his new paramour is the girlfriend of local mob boss Markos Szabo (David Dencik). Too bad that Matt just doesn’t care.

Well, that’s life in Gotham City (perpetually damp, grimy, and graffiti-covered), and when Matt and Mia wake up the next morning, they’re surrounded by Markos and his band of (lightly Dick Tracy-coded) toughs. Markos, understandably ticked off (and somehow aware that Corey had told Matt that Mia was taken), takes out all his toxic masculine rage on Matt’s gorgeous face, carving him up and leaving him to deal with it. Gross, goopy, gory, bloody, and just plain meaty , Matt’s physical ailments aren’t shied away from at all, and Watkins’ dedication to going full body horror is admirable.

And the attendant facial disfigurations are bad enough (remember, Matt is an actor, he really needs his face), but what follows is arguably worse. Believing he might find justice (in Gotham City?!), Matt tries to take legal action against Markos. What follows: character assassinations, horrific surgeries, financial lootings, and the total decimation of life as he knows it. Which is all to say, when Matt meets Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie), he’s willing to do anything to get a slice of his life back. And Caitlyn sure loves slicing, dicing, and toying with “nanocells” (not clay, sorry) that Matt believes can fix his visage.

Great news! It does! Well, for a time. Hellbent on getting his life back (via his face), Matt overdoses on those damn nanocells and promptly becomes a monster, both figuratively and literally. Gone is our sweet young actor, instead replaced by a snarling, revenge-obsessed freak who is scared (and then delighted) to discover he can shift his face into whatever he wants, whoever he wants, whenever he wants. (A subplot about how Caitlyn can calm him feels terribly shoehorned in to add an icky romance dimension.)

Increasingly muddy effects and plotting don’t do Matt’s transformations many favors — the film does much better, clever work when he’s just slipping between different faces, zipping behind a door and emerging as someone else. The mechanics of those transformations aren’t clear either: are they subconscious? does he need to think of someone to “become” them? touch them? can he make their clothes too? or is that also skin? We’re spinning out just thinking on it. At least these moments allow some supporting stars, including Eddie Marsan and James, the chance to have quite a bit of fun playing Matt “playing” their characters.

A few meaty set pieces help, too, including a truly stomach-churning sequence set on an airplane (turbulence and nanocells are a bad mix) and a third act revenge-driven visit to the club that gives Rhys Harries plenty to chew on (to say nothing of some of Matt’s biggest foes). But the uneven nature of the film, its plotting, its character motivations, and its aims only become bigger and bloodier as the film winds on. Malleable, sure, but this ambitious misfire can never conform to one shape, one final form, or one good idea.

Grade: C+

Warner Bros. will release “Clayface” in theaters on Friday, October 23.
excerpt_original: James Watkins' gory, goopy R-rated body horror is an offbeat addition to the DCU's increasingly erratic output, but it feels much more like a curiosity than an essential story.

article_text:
Jessica Edwards has been named the new executive director of the Woodstock Film Festival , the organization announced Sunday as the 27th annual festival came to a close. Edwards will take over the role from Meira Blaustein, the festival’s co-founder.

“I have had the pleasure of working with Jessica at the Woodstock Film Festival over the past few years, and I have nothing but the greatest respect for her,” said Blaustein. “As a filmmaker, a distribution consultant, and a former publicist, Jessica brings with her deep understanding, creative vision, and vast and strong contacts in the film industry. As a resident of the Hudson Valley, she knows and loves the region and its community. I am confident that she will not only retain the vision of the Woodstock Film Festival, which I have worked so long and hard to build and nurture, but will lead it towards an exciting new growth. I can’t wait to see what the next few years will bring. Welcome, Jessica!”

Related Stories

'Other Desert Cities' Broadway Review: Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Ed Harris and Allison Janney Lead a Resounding Family Drama

Claude Dal Farra, who serves as president of the festival’s board, also welcomed Edwards appointment.

Popular on Variety

“From our very first meeting with Jessica, it was clear to us that she was the natural person to succeed Meira and carry forward the extraordinary work Meira has done over more than 25 years,” she said. “Jessica understands what makes the Woodstock Film Festival special — its commitment to filmmakers, its independent spirit, and its deep connection to the Hudson Valley — while also bringing the experience, energy, and vision to lead it into its next chapter. On behalf of the Board, we are tremendously excited to welcome Jessica as our new Executive Director, and to work with her on the future of the Festival.”

Edwards shared that this role is one she considers a “dream job.” “I’m honored to build on the founders’ legacy and help shape the festival’s future,” she said. “Woodstock’s history is shaped by its creativity, innovation, and independent spirit. I want to carry that spirit forward by bringing filmmakers and industry partners from around the world together with audiences here in the Hudson Valley. My vision for the festival is to create opportunities for people to meet, share ideas, and discover films together — connections that I hope will support filmmakers and inspire the next generation of cinema lovers.”

The festival ran from Wednesday to Sunday, during which an Honorary Maverick Award was presented to Blaustein to recognize her leadership, more than 26 years of dedication to independent cinema and the legacy she has built.

Festival winners included “Mouse” by Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson, “Rehearsals for a Revolution” by Pegah Ahangarani, “Washed Up” by Isabel Moncloa Daly and “They’re Here” by Laura Poitras & Rachel Lauren Mueller.

article_text:
Anlässlich des 100-jährigen Leinwandjubiläums von Fritz Langs dystopischem Science-Fiction-Epos „Metropolis“ widmet sich die Retrospektive der kommenden Berlinale unter dem Titel „Rage Against the Machine“ filmischen Zukunftsentwürfen. Wobei als Leitmotiv die Rebellion gegen entmenschlichte, ungerechte Zustände fungiert.

Am 10. Januar 2027 jährt sich die Uraufführung eines der einflussreichsten Werke der deutschen Filmgeschichte. Denn im Winter 1927 feierte Fritz Langs „ Metropolis “ Premiere, ein Science-Fiction-Epos um eine dystopische Zukunftsstadt, das einen der ersten wichtigen Meilensteine des Genres darstellte. Nicht zuletzt die „Roboter-Maria“ – die Figur eines weiblichen Androiden, den ein sinistrer Wissenschaftler als trügerische „femme fatale“-Kopie der tugendhaften weiblichen Hauptfigur erschafft – gehört bis heute zu den vielzitierten Ikonen des Zukunftskinos.

Anlässlich des 100. Jahrestags des bahnbrechenden Stummfilmklassikers widmet sich die Retrospektive der kommenden Berlinale (10.-21.2.2026) Filmen, die in die Fußstapfen von „Metropolis“ traten und „filmische Visionen von Zukunft und Widerstand“ präsentierten, wie es in der Ankündigung heißt.

Die zwischen „Postapokalypse, Cyberpunk und politischer Allegorie“ angesiedelten Werke, die unter dem Titel „Rage Against the Machine“ versammelt werden, sind nicht nur filmhistorisch von Interesse, sondern werfen Fragen auf, die aktueller nicht sein könnten: „Wie funktionieren Autorität und Kontrolle? Steuern wir die Technologie, oder steuert sie uns? Welche Formen von Opposition und Widerstand sind möglich?“ Dabei treffen so unterschiedliche Arbeiten wie der Blockbuster „ RoboCop “ (1987) von Paul Verhoeven, der Underground-Film „ Decoder “ (1984) oder „ Die letzten Tage von Gomorrha “ (1974) von Helma Sanders-Brahms aufeinander.

Leitmotiv aller Filme, so Berlinale-Intendantin Tricia Tuttle, sei „die Rebellion: der Kampf gegen Maschinen, Systeme und künstliche Intelligenz, der feministische Aufstand gegen patriarchale Machtstrukturen sowie die Auflehnung des Individuums und von unterdrückten Gruppen gegen den Staat, Ideologien und soziale Kontrolle.“

Flankiert wird die Retro von der Ausstellung „The Metropolis Century – Dystopia and Rebellion“, die vom 18.3. bis 26.9.2027 in der Deutschen Kinemathek zu sehen sein wird.

article_text:
The Weitzman National Museum of American Jewish History in Philadelphia is being considered as a potential new member of the Smithsonian museum network, with members of a new congressional commission sworn in on Tuesday set to study the matter.

As reported by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency , Philip Darivoff, a former longtime chair of the Weitzman and current chair of the new commission, and Dara Horn, a writer serving as vice chair, “said that the Weitzman joining the Smithsonian would send a powerful message that Jews are a crucial component of the history of the country.”

Darivoff told the JTA , “It’s a different statement that our country makes when it says that the study of Jewish American history and culture is important to this nation,” and both commission members hope possible inclusion in the Smithsonian network could help stem what they called an “epidemic of ignorance” about Jewish history and culture.

The prospect of the Weitzman joining the Smithsonian dates back to legislation passed by the Biden administration in 2024 to establish the congressional commission. Now, after having been sworn in, the commission has two years to study the matter—“though Darivoff said he hopes to finish the work well before the deadline,” according to the JTA .

The Weitzman National Museum of American Jewish History was founded in 1976 and is currently a Smithsonian affiliate, which means it can share resources with other museums in the network. Current offerings there include a new “immersive family experience” called Colors of Creation, an exhibition titled “The First Salute: An Untold Story of the American Revolution,” and a core exhibition covering history dating back to the 1600s, “when the first permanent Jewish settlers came to the New World from Brazil.”

article_text:
Alex Margo Arden: Nothing Personal

★★★★☆

They tried to make her go to rehab and she said “no, no, no”. And she probably would’ve said no to letting the artist Alex Margo Arden mount an exhibition out of all her old junk, too, but sadly Amy Winehouse isn’t around to protest, so Arden’s gone ahead regardless.

In display cases and on shelves in a lush Chelsea flat, Arden has assembled a collection of objects and books based on what Winehouse once owned. Trawling through archive material and auction records, Arden has bought duplicates of Winehouse’s makeup, her copies of Vogue, her boardgames, her books.

So you get to snoop through her private junk, imagining her reading all these biographies of jazzers and celebs, or the Claudia Roden book of Jewish food. The thought of her reading Roy Keane’s autobiography while slurping down matzah-ball soup is beautiful.

Did Winehouse really do the 1,000-piece Cadbury jigsaw puzzle? Did she read the article on “the body we all want now” in that issue of Vogue? Arden is forcing you to ask these questions, imagine these scenarios, turning you into a celebrity stalker, someone who has become unable to separate idol from human.

There’s a pair of ballet pumps signed by fans and left on her doorstep after Winehouse’s death, a birthday card from Mark Ronson and Adele that she never got to open. Now we’re too close, now it feels like we’re intruding.

It’s a weirdly cold, unemotional display. But two things are opening at once here: there’s a portrait of an icon being created out of the objects and ephemera of their life, and there’s an uncomfortable exploration of the fetishisation of celebrity. There’s an act of love and devotion, and there’s an act of critical self-reflection. Joy and discomfort, rubbing awkwardly up against each other. It’s very smart, very critical conceptual art that makes you feel pretty grubby and intrusive.

Nicoletta Fiorucci Foundation, until 23 January 2027

Yuko Mohri: In Concert

★★★★☆

The Barbican has sprung a leak. Actually, it has sprung loads of them, which is why they’re investing so much in trying to repair this poor old brutalist beast.

But in Yuko Mohri’s installation, those leaks aren’t maintenance problems, they’re creative collaborators. Water drips out of sinks and pipes in the Curve, gathering in buckets and tarpaulins, being funnelled and pumped through tubes. Each drip triggers a little cymbal, a triangle, a mallet on a drum. The Barbican’s collapsing infrastructure is playing you a tune.

It’s surreal, cacophonous: repurposed Barbican lamps, flickering on and off, are being controlled by sensors measuring the moisture levels in rotting fruit, others by breezes blowing through the Barbican’s draughty walls – all at the will of mouldy fruit and crumbling concrete walls.

It’s the best use of the Curve for years: Mohri has turned rot and disrepair into an instrument and made the building’s frailties into a symphony of survival. When life gives you lemons, you make lemonade. When it gives you a leaky roof, you make musique concrète.

Barbican Curve, until 24 January 2027

Yuyan Wang: Pilgrims

★★★★☆

Light is a positive thing in popular culture. We call smart people bright, we say good things are “lit”, etc. But there’s a darkness to how Chinese artist Yuyan Wang approaches it in this new film work.

It takes as its starting point a 2018 initiative from the Chinese government to launch artificial moons in order to provide continuous daylight.

Moths and bugs flit across the screen downstairs, drawn to a lamp, their natural instincts duped by artificial light. Upstairs, found footage of drills and mines, LEDs, fireworks, lasers, rockets, torches and neon striplights flicker past, soundtracked by blasts of synthesiser choir chords. Wang is asking what it means to have no darkness, to be constantly productive, to have no rest or escape.

I guess we are the moths now, being fooled by the artificial lights of a world that treats us like bugs.

Over in the crypt of Shoreditch church next door, another video shows humanoid robots being constructed. You get the sense that Wang knows that our terrifying imminent future will just be more forgotten industrial detritus.

This is what art cinema does well: non-narrative, alluring, disconcerting weirdness.

Emalin, until 14 November

Rebecca Warren: There Will Be Another You

★★★★☆

Twenty years after her nomination for the Turner prize, Rebecca Warren has lost none of her angular, gritty, rough, weird power.

The sculptor is back for her first London show in 16 years with more of her lumpy unfired clay and bronze figures, and they are still perfectly imperfect. The smaller sculptures look like a post-apocalyptic take on decorative rococo ceramics. Instead of glistening perfection and flowing, ornamental robes, we’ve got rough, gloopy, brittle nudes stretched out on rocks. They’re funny, ugly things. But you can’t help but feel like the avalanche of faux-amateurish, kindergarten-grade ceramics that are so popular these days might all be Warren’s fault.

The big bronzes in the main space are the best. Lifesize nudes with hands and feet that have grown grotesque and lumpen, they’re somewhere between Henry Moore, Alberto Giacometti and Robert Crumb, like a bawdy grotesque take on modernism. It’s like all your favourite modernists have melted together, making one big, lumpy but pretty delicious visual soup.

Maureen Paley, until 12 December

William Kentridge: A Nicely Built City

★★★☆☆

William Kentridge is in a despairing mood. For decades, the South African artist – last seen round these parts with a major show at the Royal Academy in 2022 – has been making animated films about the fate of his home city, Johannesburg. The latest iteration is on show here, and it’s a pretty miserable thing. Whatever hope could be found in the earlier works is gone. Johannesburg has fallen further into ruin. A gas explosion has gutted a building, trees are blighted by fungus, women cradle their terrified children, protesters pack the streets, all rendered in filthy charcoal. The character of Soho Eckstein, a major industrialist in a modernist house, reappears – but now he seems to stand in for the artist, an isolated older man watching it all fall apart from the safety of his mansion.

I’ve never been much of a Kentridge fan, and this all just feels a bit too whimsical for the subject matter. But it’s still classic Kentridge: experimental, theatrical art about deeply emotional issues. It’s a small, museum-quality show filled with drawings and sculptures that will make Kentridge fans very happy but probably won’t do much to get the rest of us on side.

article_text:
Anne Imhof / Anne Imhof: House of Swans / Sep 25, 2026 – Jan 3, 2027 /

JC Contemporary / Tai Kwun / 10 Hollywood Road / Central, Hong Kong / Tue – Sun, 11am – 7pm /

taikwun.hk

Tai Kwun Contemporary presents Anne Imhof: House of Swans (25 Sep 2026 to 3 Jan 2027), on view across three floors of the JC Contemporary and F Hall galleries. Curated by Ying Kwok and Tiffany Leung, House of Swans marks the Asian solo exhibition debut of the 2017 Venice Biennale Golden Lion recipient Anne Imhof. Presenting a substantial body of new work conceived specifically for Tai Kwun, the exhibition juxtaposes her multidisciplinary artworks with sculptural elements and a soundscape of original music. Within this striking scenography, visitors explore an environment filled with suspense yet poised for action.

The exhibition foregrounds the artist’s deepening connection to classical ballet, revisiting and expanding upon her previous performance work, DOOM: House of Hope (2025). With a newly produced soundtrack incorporating classical and electronic music, House of Swans takes audiences through imposing and intimate architectural spaces to create a powerful choreography. During the exhibition’s run, performances by dancers from Hong Kong Ballet provide a window into the unfolding narrative of House of Swans , showcasing Imhof’s ongoing inquiry into bodily expression and individual transformation.

Imhof’s practice defies a single narrative; instead, it pairs contrasting elements, creating conditions for events to unfold. In House of Swans , she presents a stage for performances through large-scale installations and videos that stand alongside more traditional artistic media such as drawings, paintings and bronze reliefs. The exhibition guides visitors through artworks in suspended states between figuration and abstraction, contingency and control, and permanence and impermanence. The performances inspired by classical ballet offer one interpretation of the exhibition’s scenography.

Selected Performances

Throughout the exhibition’s run, adapted performances by Hong Kong Ballet will take place in the gallery on selected weekends in Oct and Nov. During these activations dancers move between the 3/F galleries at scheduled times to present the central refrain from a new ballet conceived by Imhof, which follows a young heroine who seeks to reclaim her power, agency and voice as a woman – both within society and on stage – as she navigates love, personal conviction and duty to her family.

The performance was developed with Devon Teuscher, Michael Dé La Nuez, Remy Young, Toon Lobach, Daniil Simkin and Eliza Douglas, alongside Qingxin Wang, Ryo Kato, Gouta Seki and the corps de ballet of Hong Kong Ballet. The ballet’s original score was commissioned from composer Jacob Madden and developed in close collaboration with Imhof, with musical contributions by Ville Haimala, Eliza Douglas, Luke Hülsmann and Levi Strasser.

Adapted Performances by Hong Kong Ballet 10, 11, 24, 25, 31 Oct 2026 1, 7, 8, 14, 15, 21, 22, 28, 29 Nov 2026 2:30pm – 3:15pm, 3:45pm – 4:30pm

Ticketing Tickets are now available online on art-mate. HK$50 (Regular Tickets) HK$40 (Concession Tickets for full-time students, seniors aged 60 or above, and persons with disabilities) Multi-Entry Pass HK$90 | Four visits and exclusive dining offers Free entry for children aged 4 or below Further ticketing information is available on the Tai Kwun Website

Learning and Engagement Programmes Over the course of the exhibition, Tai Kwun Contemporary will present a series of learning and engagement programmes such as Teachers’ Morning and Teachers’ Workshop. Held on weekends, Guided Tours: Who’s Next? offer thought-provoking perspectives on the exhibition from art professionals and guest contributors. The Tai Kwun Family Day programmes offer tours and activities for participants aged five and above, while Kids Day is scheduled in Dec. On 2/F, the Hi! & Seek corner offers a space for dialogue and exploration about the exhibition’s themes.

editorial_title_zh: 绘画方向：对埃лена·切雷蒂·斯坦（Elena Ceretti Stein）的专访
editorial_excerpt_zh: 走近这位将每幅画作视作微型生态系统、神圣事物实体化的艺术家，在她的作品中，人类重回动物状态，成为那个曾误以为自己已经超脱的世界的一部分。文章《绘画方向：对埃лена·切雷蒂·斯坦（Elena Ceretti Stein）的专访》源自……

"View 6 (After Durer), 2026年，布面油画，40×40 cm。摄影：Daniel Hanoch", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "究竟是谁对“绘画的死亡”下了定论？在全意大利的工作室里，一股年轻艺术家浪潮正在证明事实恰恰相反，他们将古典传统与我们这个时代的超连线想象力嫁接在一起。这个全新专栏致力于介绍活跃在美丽国度的青年艺术家。通过直接且不加修饰的幕后访谈，我们去发掘那些选择用世界上最古老的媒介来讲述当下复杂性的人们的痴迷与语言越界，他们的创作植根于对传统流派（从肖像画、风景画到静物画）的重新定义。我们采访了埃莱娜·切雷蒂·斯坦（Elena Ceretti Stein，1989年生于米兰），以下是我们的采访内容。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如果用几行字来形容，你今天会如何描述你的绘画探索？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我的探索在过去与现在之间牵线搭桥：我经常结合使用古老的技术（例如罩染法）以及我在多年专注于装置艺术的过程中吸收并内化的厚涂、雕塑般的材质感。从概念上讲，我的作品探讨了生态系统和生存网络的概念。对我来说，生态系统是神圣事物的实体化。而我的每一幅画作本身就是一个微型生态系统。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正因如此，我经常从现有的画作（例如文艺复兴时期的杰作）中汲取灵感，并根据需要对它们进行修改：模仿、复制、颠覆。我喜欢将来自看似遥远文化的元素混合在一起，例如将一件弗兰德斯元素与一处波斯细密画的细节并置。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些画作充满了等待、沉默和期盼，只有通过仔细观察，人们才会发现在一层颜料背后还隐藏着另一层。另一个人物、另一处风景、一扇揭示出一个期待中的世界的窗户。这些画作通常尺寸很小，就像马赛克的拼贴，其颜料质感在某些地方堆积，打破了画布的边界。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/ElenaCerettiStein_Reproductions_sep22-DanielHanochPhotographer-7-300x200.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "View 7 (After Fra Angelico), 2022年，布面油画与金箔，40×40 cm。摄影：Daniel Hanoch", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你是如何走上绘画之路的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我一直在画画。后来我学了一年绘画，但没有完成学业。我过去倾向于过于专注于技术，过于追求现实主义。因此我转向了装置艺术，以保持自由。当几年后我重回绘画时，我的绘画方式也发生了转变，而我依然感到自由。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/2MB-Nexus-300x200.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "NEXUS, 2022年，三通道视听装置", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "有哪些过去的艺术家和巨匠被你视为参考或灵感来源？在当代艺术家中，你又最关注谁？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“目前在巨匠中是安托内洛·达·梅西那（Antonello da Messina）、乔托（Giotto）和扬·凡·艾克（Jan van Eyck）。东正教圣像。巴萨万（Basawan）。在当代艺术家中，是萨拉切诺（Saraceno）和于格（Huyghe），他们虽然不是画家，但他们的探索深深地唤醒了我。我们的探索有极多的共同点。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对你来说，绘画是目的还是手段？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“每一幅画都是一窗户。画画就是把它打开。我不知道呼吸究竟是目的还是手段。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/St-Jerome_s-studio-1-225x300.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Saint Jerome’s studio (After Antonello da Messina), 2026年，木板油画，70×50 cm", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你在作品中探讨了哪些主题？为什么你认为它们在当下如此重要？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“正如我所说，我谈论的是生态系统，而谈论生态系统就必然涉及平衡、转变以及生死。我试图将人类重新带回那个他不断试图自欺欺人地逃离的世界中。我将他带回其动物性之中，带回他作为整体一部分的属性中。我通常通过描绘场所来做到这一点：每个房间、每个空间都是一个系统、一个微观宇宙，文化在那里相互吞噬、相互交织，生物学构成了本质的一部分。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在你看来，哪些元素是你的绘画方式中不可或缺的（例如色彩、笔触、构图、材质、技术）？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“层叠法与色彩的运用。我花极长的时间在色彩上。某些色彩你看不见，但你能感受到它们。它们潜藏在画布的表层之下。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Photo-of-whole-space-Elena-Ceretti-Stein-300x225.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "展览“Where Paths Meet”现场图，当代艺术中心，拉姆拉，2023年。摄影：Daniele Lazzaretto", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当代语境（社会、文化或政治）对你的作品有多大影响？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“有时我把我的画作当作躲避世事的地方。逃离或回归的房间。内在宗教的圣像。尽管我的探索并非明确的政治性，但它围绕着这样一种愿望展开：不再聚焦于单个元素去感知世界，而是聚焦于系统及其互动。以相互依赖和涌现属性为钥匙的生存之道。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Four-women-front-view-Installation-OFFSPRING-2024-1-300x200.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "展览现场图，The Four Women，Ncontemporary画廊，2024年。摄影：Daniele Lazzaretto", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在你的创作过程中，你是否会使用数码工具或人工智能？如果是，以什么方式？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我既不用人工智能来画画，也不用它来写像这样的文本，事实上这篇文章充满了不完美以及我本可以写得更好的地方。我曾尝试用它来生成画作的局部，但行不通：结果总是非常媚俗。我确实会谨慎地使用人工智能，主要将其作为财务规划工具。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哪些绘画之外的影响（例如电影、音乐、文学、网络图像等）最常出现在你的作品中？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“通常是科学研究。例如，我的最新展览（SUNBURN）聚焦于一些在意大利领土上被视为入侵物种的昆虫，比如日本弧丽金龟（Popillia japonica）。此外，我也会使用我在网络上遇到的图像。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Popillia-Japonica-225x300.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Popillia Japonica (lady holding leaf), 2026年，木板油画，70×50厘米。由 Braverman 画廊提供。摄影：Elad Sarig", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在你的工作中，个人经验和集体经验占有多大的空间？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "«这些画作反映了这两种经验，并且不仅仅是从人类中心主义的视角出发。它们有时会以一种非等级的方式探索非人类生物及元素的集体和个体经验，以及它们与人类的关系。»", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在创作一件作品的过程中，你认为哪个时刻最重要，它又是如何影响最终结果的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "«通常在创作一件作品的最初几个小时里，会有一些自发的笔触为画作指明方向。某种粗粝的能量凝聚下来，为接下来的笔触奠定基调，哪怕是几天或几个月后出现的那些更为细腻的笔触也是如此。事后修改要困难得多。我们必须努力营造正确的开端，犯下正确的错误。»", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Ceratocystis-Platanii-225x300.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Ceratocystis Platani, 2026年，布面油画，42×32厘米。由 Braverman 画廊提供。摄影：Elad Sarig", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你何时决定一件作品已经完成了？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "«决定这一点总是很难。我通常觉得它完成了，是因为字面意义上我再也不知道该修改什么了。这是一种身体上的感觉。就像手拒绝去寻找还能往哪里画下去一样。就像汽油耗尽了一样。»", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在当下的语境中，是什么促使你今天选择绘画？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "«我经常通过我的绘画来创作装置、物件和雕塑。我对绘画的体验非常流畅。它的不朽、原始和本质深深吸引着我。对我来说，绘画是一种自然的、与生俱来的本能。»", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": article_text:
Chi l’ha proferita l’ultima parola sulla “morte della pittura”? Negli atelier di tutta Italia, una wave di giovani artisti sta dimostrando l’esatto contrario, innestando la tradizione classica all’immaginario iper-connesso dei nostri giorni. Questa nuova rubrica è dedicata ai pittori emergenti attivi nel Bel Paese. Attraverso interviste dirette e senza filtri dietro le quinte della loro ricerca, andiamo a scoprire le ossessioni, gli sconfinamenti linguistici di chi ha scelto il medium più antico del mondo per raccontare la complessità del presente, nel solco di una ridefinizione dei generi tradizionali, dal ritratto al paesaggio e alla natura morta. Abbiamo incontrato Elena Ceretti Stein (Milano, 1989), qui la nostra intervista.

Come descriveresti oggi, in poche righe, la tua ricerca pittorica?

«La mia ricerca tende i fili tra passato e presente: spesso uso un mix di tecniche antiche, come le velature, e una componente materica, scultorea, che ho assorbito e metabolizzato dedicandomi per molti anni alle installazioni. Concettualmente il mio lavoro si interroga sull’idea di ecosistema, di una rete dell’esistenza. Per me un ecosistema è la materializzazione del sacro. E ognuno dei miei quadri è in se stesso un piccolo ecosistema.

Per questo spesso mi ispiro a quadri già esistenti (per esempio capolavori rinascimentali) modificandoli come mi conviene: imitandoli, copiandoli, stravolgendoli. Amo mischiare elementi provenienti da culture apparentemente lontane, per esempio accostando un elemento fiammingo al dettaglio di una miniatura persiana.

Sono quadri pieni di attesa, di silenzio, di anticipazione, dove solo osservando con attenzione ci si accorge che dietro a uno strato di colore se ne nasconde un altro. Un’altra figura, un altro paesaggio, una finestra che rivela un mondo in attesa. Sono quadri spesso di piccolo formato, come tessere di un mosaico, con un impasto che in alcuni punti si accumula, liberandosi dei confini della tela.»

Come ti sei avvicinata alla pittura?

«Ho sempre disegnato. Poi ho studiato pittura per un anno, ma non ho completato gli studi. Avevo la tendenza a concentrarmi troppo sulla tecnica, a essere troppo realista. Così mi sono dedicata alle installazioni, per restare libera. Quando sono tornata alla pittura, anni dopo, si era trasformato anche il mio modo di dipingere, e ho continuato a sentirmi libera.»

Quali sono gli artisti e maestri del passato che senti come riferimenti o punti di ispirazione? E tra i contemporanei, chi segui con maggiore interesse?

«In questo momento, tra i maestri, Antonello da Messina, Giotto e Jan van Eyck. Le icone ortodosse. Basawan. Tra i contemporanei, Saraceno e Huyghe, che non sono pittori, ma la loro ricerca mi attiva profondamente. Le nostre ricerche hanno moltissimo in comune.»

La pittura per te è un fine o un mezzo?

«Ogni quadro è una finestra. Dipingere è aprirla. Non so se respirare sia un fine o un mezzo.»

Quali temi affronti nel tuo lavoro e perché li ritieni importanti in questo momento?

«Come dicevo, parlo di ecosistemi e, parlando di ecosistemi, si parla necessariamente di equilibrio, di trasformazioni e di vita-morte. Cerco di riportare l’uomo dentro al mondo dal quale cerca continuamente di illudersi di essere uscito. Lo riporto nel suo essere animale, nel suo essere parte del tutto. Spesso lo faccio dipingendo luoghi: ogni stanza, ogni spazio è un sistema, un microuniverso, dove le culture si mangiano e si intersecano, dove la biologia è parte dell’essenza.»

Quali elementi consideri fondamentali nel tuo modo di dipingere (ad esempio colore, segno, composizione, materia, tecnica)?

«L’uso degli strati e del colore. Passo un tempo lunghissimo a lavorare sul colore. Certi colori non li vedi, ma li senti. Stanno dietro agli strati superficiali della tela.»

Quanto influisce il contesto contemporaneo (sociale, culturale o politico) sul tuo lavoro?

«A volte uso i miei quadri come luoghi in cui nascondermi dagli eventi del mondo. Stanze dalle quali evadere, o nelle quali tornare. Icone di una religione interna. Seppur non esplicitamente politica, la mia ricerca ruota attorno alla voglia di percepire il mondo non più concentrandomi sui singoli elementi, ma sui sistemi e sulla loro interazione. La sopravvivenza in chiave di interdipendenza e di proprietà emergenti.»

Utilizzi strumenti digitali o intelligenza artificiale nel tuo processo creativo? Se sì, in che modo?

«Non uso l’AI per i quadri e neanche per i testi come questo, che infatti è pieno di imperfezioni e cose che avrei potuto scrivere meglio. Ho provato con pezzi di quadro, ma non funziona: i risultati sono sempre stati molto kitsch. Uso l’AI, con parsimonia, principalmente come strumento di pianificazione finanziaria.»

Quali influssi esterni alla pittura (per esempio cinema, musica, letteratura, immagini online, ecc.) sono più presenti nel tuo lavoro?

«Spesso studi scientifici. La mia ultima mostra ( SUNBURN ) si concentra, per esempio, su alcuni insetti che sono considerati specie invasive sul territorio italiano, come la Popillia japonica . Poi uso le immagini che incontro online.»

Nel tuo lavoro quanto spazio hanno l’esperienza personale e quella collettiva?

«I quadri riflettono entrambe le esperienze, e non solo dal punto di vista antropocentrico, umano. A volte esplorano le esperienze collettive e individuali di creature ed elementi non umani e la loro relazione con gli umani, in maniera non gerarchica.»

Durante la realizzazione di un’opera, qual è il momento che consideri più importante e come incide sul risultato finale?

«Spesso nelle prime ore di lavoro su un’opera ci sono alcune pennellate spontanee che segnano il percorso del quadro. Si condensa una certa energia grezza che imposta le pennellate successive, anche quelle molto più dettagliate che arrivano nei giorni o mesi successivi. Correggere in seguito è molto più difficile. Bisogna sforzarsi di creare l’inizio giusto e di fare gli errori giusti.»

Quando decidi che un’opera è conclusa?

«È sempre difficile decidere. Spesso sento che è conclusa quando letteralmente non so più cosa modificare. È una sensazione fisica. Come se la mano si rifiutasse di trovare dove andare avanti. Come se finisse la benzina.»

Cosa ti porta a scegliere la pittura oggi, nel contesto contemporaneo?

«Spesso con la mia pittura creo installazioni, oggetti, sculture. Vivo la pittura in maniera molto fluida. Mi attira il suo essere immortale, primitiva, essenziale. Dipingere per me è un istinto naturale, innato.»

Pensi che il valore della tua opera possa variare all’interno di una grande mostra collettiva come Ensemble ? In che modo?

«Non è facile per la mia opera di formato 40 × 40, non figurativa, trovare il proprio spazio in una grande collettiva in cui sono protagonisti quadri di grandi dimensioni, dai colori forti, ritratti e figurativi. Il quadro in mostra è una stanza vuota, dai colori tenui. Un paesaggio sospeso che richiede un certo vuoto attorno, un certo silenzio. È un’opera che di proposito non si impone, non grida. Si appoggia al bianco che la circonda, creando uno spazio che risucchia. Sarà interessante vederla dialogare con universi e voci diverse.»

Sawayama）担任策展人。该展览是摄影两百周年（Bicentennial of Photography）庆祝活动的一部分，2026年标志着摄影术发明200周年。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览伴随着泽山辽（Ryo Sawayama）关于这位艺术家作品的这篇评论文章。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "1963年，20岁的杉浦邦惠从日本移居美国，并入读芝加哥艺术学院（School of the Art Institute of Chicago）——这是一所传承自新包豪斯（New Bauhaus）脉络的机构。正是在芝加哥，杉浦首次接触到作为媒介的摄影，并开启了她的艺术家生涯。自那时起，杉浦一直将摄影作为她的主要创作媒介。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在当时，摄影在艺术界仍被视为一种次要领域，从属于绘画和雕塑。直到后来，一批女性艺术家——如辛迪·舍曼（Cindy Sherman）、弗兰西斯卡·伍德曼（Francesca Woodman）、安娜·门迪埃塔（Ana Mendieta）、劳瑞·西蒙斯（Laurie Simmons）、芭芭拉·克鲁格（Barbara Kruger）等——才将摄影作为重要的媒介。杉浦的作品预示了这一转变（可以在贝蒂·哈恩（Betty Hahn）身上找到同时代的平行案例）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "女性艺术家之所以积极采用摄影，恰恰是因为它长期以来被贬低为一种次要的表现方式。与绘画和雕塑这些主要由男性艺术家占据的传统领域不同，摄影被视为一个向边缘人群开放的民主领域。因此，身为外国人和女性的杉浦将摄影作为自己的媒介，是一个植根于这些议题之中的有意识且具理论性的选择。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管杉浦将摄影确立为她的主要媒介，但她一直刻意与那些同直摄（straight photography）相关的所谓“摄影作品”保持距离，同样也不愿被视作一名“摄影师”。相反，杉浦不断追求并拓展摄影内在的潜在造型性，试验摄影如何成为一种能够与绘画和雕塑相媲美的表达方式。杉浦的作品并不把摄影视作一种享有特权的媒介本身；它是通过杂交（hybridization）以及与其他媒介的结合来介入摄影的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "杂交的运用体现在杉浦于1971年创作的《光画布岛2》（Photocanvas Island 2）中，在这件作品里，摄影与绘画结合在了一起。在这里，丙烯颜料被层叠在康尼岛防波堤表面的照片之上，被拍摄防波堤粗糙的“基底”叠加到了绘画的“基底”之上，笔触与岩石表面原有的纹理相结合。防波堤的三维客体与二维的画面、具象与抽象在此交织。在这里，杉浦并没有自由挥洒笔触，而是沿着岩石已经形成的纹理和图案来安排它们。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对杉浦而言，摄影与绘画的结合意味着与既有的自然进行合作：创造一种自然与人工的叠加。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种结合贯穿于杉浦的整个创作生涯：摄影与绘画在《岛2》（Island 2，1971年）、《圣诞灯饰》（Christmas Lights，1979年）和《细泽》（Hossawa，2022年）中的结合；多个画幅在《有田与宫崎》（Arita and Miyazaki，均为2023年）中的结合；不同序列在《鲶鱼的故事》（Story of Catfish，1993年）中的连接；通过X光摄影在《椎骨》（Vertebra，2021年）和《架子》（Racks，1994年）中将骨骼结构与关节相连，其中容纳明信片大小X光照片的照片架让人联想到骨骼的连接结构或DNA结构。这种结合还可见于杉浦用线将花朵捆绑在一起的作品，或是表现一对夫妇做爱的巨幅光画布。在杉浦的作品中，摄影是一种造型材料，它对与其接触的一切进行着无休止的分割与结合操作。通过这些结合，新的形态得以产生。通过策划这些相遇、结合和杂交，杉浦将摄影变成了一个实验场所，展现出其开放、横向和中介的本质。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "杉浦在日本也作为作家广为人知，曾在《美术手帖》上开设固定专栏。在互联网普及之前，她自1980年代起从纽约发出的信息极其宝贵。杉浦将纽约的艺术界介绍到日本，在自己的工作室里接待并照顾了许多日本访客，将他们与当地艺术社区的实地人士连接起来——她本人在各个意义上都是一位调解者。杉浦比任何人都更深刻地理解到，事物之间的相遇会产生新的形式，而偶然的相遇则会引发新的事件。从某种意义上说，杉浦作为调解者的立场，与她对待摄影这一媒介的态度如出一辙。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "杉浦的作品传承了新包豪斯的思考模式，将摄影与各种其他媒介交叉并结合，这与她将摄影视为形式实验场的处理方式相辅相成。其实践的特点在于它与早期实验摄影和先锋摄影的连续性——通过使用摄影ogram（光影拼图）、X光照片以及对感光乳剂的物质性与流体性运用。杉浦对待摄影的方式，不仅仅是将其作为复制现有场景的手段，而是将其视为形式发明的实验田。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "实验与前卫摄影恰恰探索了摄影内在的这种可塑潜力，而此类实验的前身则是包括早期灵异摄影在内的神秘摄影。值得一提的是，摄影的诞生与精神主义的兴起在历史上是同时发生的。湿版和干版的多次曝光、污渍、化学不均匀性以及显影过程中的不规则还原反应，常常会产生意想不到的双重影像或朦胧形态。这使得不同的时间片段得以在同一个画幅空间中共存，正如未来主义绘画中那样（尽管更准确地说，未来主义绘画受到的是实验摄影的影响，而非相反）。这些摄影工艺及其不可预测的效果，都在拓展摄影的可塑潜力方面发挥了作用。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在当时，人们认为摄影无需人为干预，便能自动且客观地显现出幽灵的存在。前卫与实验摄影有意识且在美学上重新启用了最早见于早期灵异摄影的技术：多次曝光、中途曝光（solarization）以及无镜头摄影（photogram）。因此，可以说灵异摄影在实验摄影和前卫艺术之前，就已经实现了摄影的化学可塑性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "可以说，摄影宣告了另一个“自然”——平行世界的存在。摄影揭示出，可感知的世界与超自然的世界相平行，并与一个超越人类感知、包含诸如紫外线和X射线等电磁波的世界并行不悖。X射线摄影精准地视觉化了可见事物背后隐藏着超越人类感知现实这一事实。通过化学结合多种物质，摄影证明了世界是多重宇宙的叠加与结合，超越了人类所能连贯理解的范畴。通过当代科学的发展和早期摄影，人们逐渐清晰地认识到，人类理解世界的方式不过是一种偶然生成的模式——一种主观上的权宜之计。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "早期摄影曾用作警察记录的证据以及历史文献的一种形式。然而与此同时，其混合挥发性物质的化学过程以及揭示原本不可见之物的能力，也赋予了早期摄影一种神奇的、甚至是可疑的特质。摄影和灵异摄影正是通过这种同样不可预测的显影过程紧密相连。“神秘（occult）”一词带有“隐藏的知识”之意。从这个意义上说，神秘摄影力求使一个隐匿的、隐藏的世界——世界的潜在可塑性及其隐藏的创造力——显现出来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正是这种期待——即摄影拥有能够揭示一个隐藏的超现实世界的自动化机制、一种独立于人类行为的自动生产力——深深吸引了将自动化（automatism）置于其方法论核心的超现实主义者，使他们对摄影产生了极大的兴趣。摄影中通过化学反应呈现图像的过程，与灵媒（spirit medium）有着相同的结构，灵媒同样使不可见之物变得可见。因此，从该词的双重含义来看，摄影堪称完美的媒介。凭借其化学可塑性，摄影将不同的世界结合在一起，并揭示出另一个不可见的自然。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "通过这种方式，摄影将一个隐藏的世界传递到当下。例如，杉浦的《小猫文件》（1992）是通过将两只小猫单独留在暗室里一周，并将它们留下的痕迹——它们的足迹和运动——转化为作品本身而创作的。这些痕迹并非由艺术家本人制造，而是由猫依照自己的意志移动所留下的；它们记录了猫超出人类意图的、不可预测的动作。这种装置——暗室里的一猫——让人联想起量子力学中的思想实验“薛定谔的猫”，其中一只被密封在箱子里的猫被描述为既活又死——一个处于量子叠加态的物体。在这里，箱子里的内容物构成了一个字面意义上的“黑盒”，在打开箱子之前，猫是生是死无从得知。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管薛定谔的猫是对量子力学中测量的不确定性进行建模的思想实验，但杉浦的《小猫文件》却是在暗室中切实执行的实验。在本次展览所展出的作品中，杉浦在同一时期创作的《鲶鱼的故事》也属于相同的艺术轨迹。无论是《小猫文件》还是《鲶鱼的故事》，暗室中动物行为所产生的那种无法控制的、概率性的偏差积累，都表现为固定在相纸上的物质痕迹。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "需要指出的一个重要点是，《小猫文件》中的“文件（Papers）”一词唤起了这样一种文献实践：即根据其物质痕迹——一个无人观察到的自然运动——在事后来重建一个事件。在这里，杉浦同时兼任创作者和观察者双重角色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "铃木崇的摄影ogram（无镜头摄影作品）在处理暗室中生物的物理运动时，揭示了自然中可能存在的无数偏差——多重世界的叠加。这些生物不受约束的运动和能量之所以产生，并非因为世界是固定且静态的，而是因为无数的可能性在其中依然潜藏且开放。正因为这些无数的世界同时叠加，世界才具备了创造力。在这里，生物不仅仅是被拍摄的对象，它本身就是产生影像的主体。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "铃木崇反复选择生命体（如人类、动物和花卉）作为拍摄对象，这与她对自然形态形成的兴趣不谋而合。通过自身能动性产生自身形态的生命体，在结构上类似于同样能自动产生影像的摄影（例如，花朵靠自身的力量生长，完全凭自身的力量形成其作为花朵的形状）。正如铃木崇本人所说，花朵是一个生殖器官：雄蕊产生花粉，雌蕊接收该花粉以创造最终成为种子的新生命。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "铃木崇将花朵用线捆绑在一起的作品，相当直观地展现了生物生殖过程中雄与雌的结合——授粉与受精。在这里，摄影的自动化机制回应了自然自我形成的进程。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在物质层面上，感光乳剂本身就是一种强行将原本无法自然相溶的物质进行均匀分散和悬浮的混合物——由水基明胶和微细银盐颗粒组成。摄影的载体本身就在物质层面上体现了异质元素之间的结合，因为摄影是通过一种将化学性质上天生无法混合的事物结合在一起的操作——即乳剂化——而诞生的。这种操作让人联想到印度教关于“搅乳海”的创世神话，其中各种植物和种子都被放入乳海中进行搅动，从这种搅动中诞生了太阳、月亮、诸神和所有的动物。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种在生殖和摄影中的结合也可以与炼金术术语 coniunctio 相联系。在炼金术过程中，所谓的“神圣婚礼”（chymical wedding）——对立面即硫磺（男性原则）与水银（女性原则）的化学结合——据说能产生一种新物质：哲人石。Coniunctio 既指化学结合，同时也作为两性结合隐喻。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "异质元素的混合与交融——乳剂化——可以被看作是生命本身的涌现。人体、生命体、花卉以及地球本身——这些铃木崇持续捕捉的主题——恰恰属于自然与生命体的这一领域，她将摄影自身形成的化学过程以及她自己的绘画和影像创作行为叠加其上。摄影与其说是一种复制手段，不如说是一种自我生成的运动，它通过结合行为生成新的形式——释放出世界本身固有的创造性生产力。铃木崇的作品揭示了一种弥漫于世界的自动创造力量的无处不在。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "铃木崇出生于日本，自1967年起常驻纽约，在过去的六十多年里，她创作了一系列跨越摄影、绘画和雕塑交叉领域的作品。《Ubiquitous Conjunction》通过精选过去六十年间创作的作品，回顾了一种从未停止突破摄影媒介边界并探索其与其它艺术形式对话可能性的艺术实践。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "泽山辽", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "泽山辽 策展", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "铃木崇：无处不在的结合 2026年10月19日 – 12月31日 弗兰克·埃尔巴兹画廊（Galerie Frank Elbaz） 66 rue de Turenne 75003 巴黎 – 法国 电话：+33 1 48 87 50 04 www.galeriefrankelbaz.com", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Galerie Frank Elbaz announces Ubiquitous Conjunction , the first solo exhibition of Kunié Sugiura in Paris, presented at the gallery from October 19 to December 31, 2026, and curated by Ryo Sawayama. The exhibition is part of the celebrations of the Bicentennial of Photography, which in 2026 mark 200 years since the invention of photography."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The exhibition is accompanied by this essay by Ryo Sawayama on the artist’s work."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In 1963, at the age of twenty, Kunié Sugiura moved from Japan to the United States and enrolled at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago—an institution which descends from the New Bauhaus lineage. It was in Chicago that Sugiura first encountered photography as a medium and began her career as an artist. From that point on, Sugiura has consistently worked with photography as her primary medium."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the time, photography was still regarded within the art world as a secondary field, subordinate to painting and sculpture. It was only later that a number of women artists—such as Cindy Sherman, Francesca Woodman, Ana Mendieta, Laurie Simmons, Barbara Kruger, among others—would take up photography as an important medium. Sugiura’s work anticipated this shift (a contemporary parallel can be found in Betty Hahn)."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Photography came to be actively taken up by women artists precisely because it had long been dismissed as a secondary mode of expression. Unlike painting and sculpture, traditional fields largely occupied by male artists, photography was seen as a democratic field open to those on the margins. Therefore, Sugiura—a foreigner and a woman—turning to photography as her medium was a conscious and theoretical choice bound up in these very issues."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Although Sugiura embraced photography as her primary medium, she has distanced herself from presenting so-called “photographic works” associated with straight photography, and likewise from being regarded as a “photographer.” Instead, Sugiura has continued to pursue and expand the latent plasticity inherent in photography, experimenting with how photography might become a means of expression equal to painting and sculpture. Sugiura’s work does not treat photography as a privileged medium in itself; it engages photography through hybridization and its conjunction with other media."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The use of hybridization can be seen in Sugiura’s Photocanvas Island 2 (1971), where photography conjoins with painting. Here, acrylic paint is layered over a photograph of the surface of the Coney Island breakwater, where the rough “ground” of the photographed breakwater is superimposed onto the “ground” of the painting, and the brushstrokes are combined with the pre-existing pattern of the rock surface. The three-dimensional object of the breakwater and the two-dimensional picture plane, the figurative and the abstract, are brought into conjunction. Here, rather than placing the brushstrokes freely, Sugiura arranges them along the textures and patterns already formed by the rocks."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For Sugiura, the conjunction of photography and painting meant collaborating with an already-existing nature: creating a superposition of nature and artifice."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This kind of conjunction can be found throughout Sugiura’s work: the conjunction of photography and painting in Island 2 (1971), Christmas Lights (1979) and Hossawa (2022); the conjunction of multiple frames in Arita and Miyazaki (both 2023); the connection of different sequences in Story of Catfish (1993); the linking of skeletal structure and joints through X-ray photography in Vertebra (2021) and Racks (1994), in which a photo rack holding postcard-sized X-ray photographs recalls the connective structure of bones, or the structure of DNA. This conjunction can also be seen where Sugiura binds flowers together with thread, or in the large photocanvas of a couple having sex. In Sugiura’s work, photography is a plastic material that carries out endless operations of severance and conjunction with everything it touches. Through these conjunctions, new forms are produced. By staging these encounters, conjunctions, and hybridizations, Sugiura turned photography into a site of experimentation, revealing its open, transversal, and mediating nature."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sugiura was also known in Japan as a writer, with a regular column in Bijutsu Techō . Before the widespread use of the internet, the information she sent from New York, from the 1980s onward, was extremely valuable. Sugiura introduced the New York art scene to Japan, welcomed and looked after many Japanese visitors in her studio, and connected them with people on the ground in the local art community—she was herself a mediator in every sense. Sugiura understood, better than anyone, that the encounter between two things generates a new form, and that chance encounters give rise to new events. In a sense, Sugiura’s stance as a mediator resembles the very attitude she takes toward photography as a medium."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sugiura’s work carries forward a New Bauhaus mode of thinking that crosses and conjoins photography with a variety of other media, in parallel with her treatment of photography as a site of formal experimentation. What characterizes her practice is its continuity with early experimental and avant-garde photography—through the use of photograms, X-ray photographs and the material and fluid use of photographic emulsion. Sugiura treats photography not simply as a means of reproducing an existing scene, but as an experimental field for formal invention."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Experimental and avant-garde photography explored precisely this plastic potential inherent in photography, and such experiments were themselves preceded by occult photography, including early spirit photography. Notably, the birth of photography and the rise of spiritualism were historically contemporaneous. Multiple exposures on wet and dry plates, stains, chemical unevenness, and irregular reduction reactions during development often produced unexpected double images or hazy forms. This made it possible for different moments in time to coexist within the same pictorial space, as in Futurist painting (although, more precisely, Futurist painting was influenced by experimental photography, rather than the reverse). These photographic processes and their unpredictable effects all served to expand photography’s plastic potential."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the time, photography was believed to reveal the presence of spirits automatically and objectively, without human intervention. Avant-garde and experimental photography consciously and aesthetically repurposed techniques first seen in early spirit photography: multiple exposure, solarization and the photogram. Therefore, it could be said that spirit photography had already realized photography’s chemical plasticity, preceding experimental photography and the avant-garde."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One could say that photography announces the existence of another “nature”—a parallel world. Photography reveals that the perceivable world runs parallel to a supernatural world, and to a world beyond human perception, that includes electromagnetic waves such as ultraviolet light and X-rays. X-ray photography visualizes precisely that behind the visible lies a reality beyond human perception. By chemically combining multiple substances, photography demonstrates that the world is a superimposition and conjunction of multiple universes, exceeding what human beings can coherently grasp. Through developments in contemporary science and early photography, it became clear that the way human beings had grasped the world was no more than a contingently generated pattern—a subjective convenience."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Early photography served as evidence in police records and as a form of historical documentation. At the same time, however, its chemical process of mixing volatile substances and its capacity to reveal what would otherwise be invisible gave early photography a magical, even suspect quality. Photography and spirit photography were bound together by this same unpredictable process of development. The word “occult” carries the meaning of “hidden knowledge.” In this sense, occult photography sought to make visible an invisible, hidden world—the latent plasticity of the world and its hidden creativity."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It was this expectation—that photography possessed an automatism capable of revealing a hidden, surreal world, an automatic productive force independent of human agency—that drew the Surrealists, who placed automatism at the center of their methodology, so intensely to photography. The emergence of an image through chemical reactions in photography shares the same structure as a spirit medium, who similarly makes the invisible visible. Photography is thus the perfect medium, in both senses of the word. Through its chemical plasticity, photography binds together different worlds and reveals another, invisible nature."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In this way, photography transmits a hidden world into the here and now. For example, Sugiura’s The Kitten Papers (1992) was made by leaving two kittens alone in a darkroom for a week and turning the traces they left—their footprints and movements—into the work itself. The traces are made not by the artist but by cats moving of their own will; they record the cats’ unpredictable movements, which are beyond human intention. This device—a cat in a darkroom—recalls the thought experiment in quantum mechanics known as “Schrödinger’s cat”, in which a cat sealed inside a box is described as simultaneously alive and dead—an object in quantum superposition. Here the contents of the box constitute a literal “black box”, and whether the cat is alive or dead cannot be known until the box is opened."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Although Schrödinger’s cat is a thought experiment modeling the indeterminacy of measurement in quantum mechanics, Sugiura’s The Kitten Papers is an experiment actually carried out in a darkroom. Among the works exhibited in this exhibition, Story of Catfish , made by Sugiura during the same period, belongs to the same artistic trajectory. In both The Kitten Papers and Story of Catfish , the accumulation of uncontrollable, probabilistic deviations produced by the behavior of animals in the darkroom appears as material traces fixed onto photographic paper."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "An important point to note is that the word “Papers” in The Kitten Papers evokes the documentary practice of reconstructing an event after the fact from its material traces—a movement of nature that no one observed. Here, Sugiura functions simultaneously as the maker and observer."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sugiura’s photograms, in dealing with the physical movement of living creatures in the darkroom, reveal the countless deviations possible within nature—the superposition of multiple worlds. The unrestrained movement and energy of these creatures arise not because the world is fixed and static, but because countless possibilities remain latent and open within it. It is because these innumerable worlds are superimposed simultaneously, that the world possesses creativity. article_text:
Galerie Frank Elbaz announces Ubiquitous Conjunction , the first solo exhibition of Kunié Sugiura in Paris, presented at the gallery from October 19 to December 31, 2026, and curated by Ryo Sawayama. The exhibition is part of the celebrations of the Bicentennial of Photography, which in 2026 mark 200 years since the invention of photography.

The exhibition is accompanied by this essay by Ryo Sawayama on the artist’s work.

In 1963, at the age of twenty, Kunié Sugiura moved from Japan to the United States and enrolled at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago—an institution which descends from the New Bauhaus lineage. It was in Chicago that Sugiura first encountered photography as a medium and began her career as an artist. From that point on, Sugiura has consistently worked with photography as her primary medium.

At the time, photography was still regarded within the art world as a secondary field, subordinate to painting and sculpture. It was only later that a number of women artists—such as Cindy Sherman, Francesca Woodman, Ana Mendieta, Laurie Simmons, Barbara Kruger, among others—would take up photography as an important medium. Sugiura’s work anticipated this shift (a contemporary parallel can be found in Betty Hahn).

Photography came to be actively taken up by women artists precisely because it had long been dismissed as a secondary mode of expression. Unlike painting and sculpture, traditional fields largely occupied by male artists, photography was seen as a democratic field open to those on the margins. Therefore, Sugiura—a foreigner and a woman—turning to photography as her medium was a conscious and theoretical choice bound up in these very issues.

Although Sugiura embraced photography as her primary medium, she has distanced herself from presenting so-called “photographic works” associated with straight photography, and likewise from being regarded as a “photographer.” Instead, Sugiura has continued to pursue and expand the latent plasticity inherent in photography, experimenting with how photography might become a means of expression equal to painting and sculpture. Sugiura’s work does not treat photography as a privileged medium in itself; it engages photography through hybridization and its conjunction with other media.

The use of hybridization can be seen in Sugiura’s Photocanvas Island 2 (1971), where photography conjoins with painting. Here, acrylic paint is layered over a photograph of the surface of the Coney Island breakwater, where the rough “ground” of the photographed breakwater is superimposed onto the “ground” of the painting, and the brushstrokes are combined with the pre-existing pattern of the rock surface. The three-dimensional object of the breakwater and the two-dimensional picture plane, the figurative and the abstract, are brought into conjunction. Here, rather than placing the brushstrokes freely, Sugiura arranges them along the textures and patterns already formed by the rocks.

For Sugiura, the conjunction of photography and painting meant collaborating with an already-existing nature: creating a superposition of nature and artifice.

This kind of conjunction can be found throughout Sugiura’s work: the conjunction of photography and painting in Island 2 (1971), Christmas Lights (1979) and Hossawa (2022); the conjunction of multiple frames in Arita and Miyazaki (both 2023); the connection of different sequences in Story of Catfish (1993); the linking of skeletal structure and joints through X-ray photography in Vertebra (2021) and Racks (1994), in which a photo rack holding postcard-sized X-ray photographs recalls the connective structure of bones, or the structure of DNA. This conjunction can also be seen where Sugiura binds flowers together with thread, or in the large photocanvas of a couple having sex. In Sugiura’s work, photography is a plastic material that carries out endless operations of severance and conjunction with everything it touches. Through these conjunctions, new forms are produced. By staging these encounters, conjunctions, and hybridizations, Sugiura turned photography into a site of experimentation, revealing its open, transversal, and mediating nature.

Sugiura was also known in Japan as a writer, with a regular column in Bijutsu Techō . Before the widespread use of the internet, the information she sent from New York, from the 1980s onward, was extremely valuable. Sugiura introduced the New York art scene to Japan, welcomed and looked after many Japanese visitors in her studio, and connected them with people on the ground in the local art community—she was herself a mediator in every sense. Sugiura understood, better than anyone, that the encounter between two things generates a new form, and that chance encounters give rise to new events. In a sense, Sugiura’s stance as a mediator resembles the very attitude she takes toward photography as a medium.

Sugiura’s work carries forward a New Bauhaus mode of thinking that crosses and conjoins photography with a variety of other media, in parallel with her treatment of photography as a site of formal experimentation. What characterizes her practice is its continuity with early experimental and avant-garde photography—through the use of photograms, X-ray photographs and the material and fluid use of photographic emulsion. Sugiura treats photography not simply as a means of reproducing an existing scene, but as an experimental field for formal invention.

Experimental and avant-garde photography explored precisely this plastic potential inherent in photography, and such experiments were themselves preceded by occult photography, including early spirit photography. Notably, the birth of photography and the rise of spiritualism were historically contemporaneous. Multiple exposures on wet and dry plates, stains, chemical unevenness, and irregular reduction reactions during development often produced unexpected double images or hazy forms. This made it possible for different moments in time to coexist within the same pictorial space, as in Futurist painting (although, more precisely, Futurist painting was influenced by experimental photography, rather than the reverse). These photographic processes and their unpredictable effects all served to expand photography’s plastic potential.

At the time, photography was believed to reveal the presence of spirits automatically and objectively, without human intervention. Avant-garde and experimental photography consciously and aesthetically repurposed techniques first seen in early spirit photography: multiple exposure, solarization and the photogram. Therefore, it could be said that spirit photography had already realized photography’s chemical plasticity, preceding experimental photography and the avant-garde.

One could say that photography announces the existence of another “nature”—a parallel world. Photography reveals that the perceivable world runs parallel to a supernatural world, and to a world beyond human perception, that includes electromagnetic waves such as ultraviolet light and X-rays. X-ray photography visualizes precisely that behind the visible lies a reality beyond human perception. By chemically combining multiple substances, photography demonstrates that the world is a superimposition and conjunction of multiple universes, exceeding what human beings can coherently grasp. Through developments in contemporary science and early photography, it became clear that the way human beings had grasped the world was no more than a contingently generated pattern—a subjective convenience.

Early photography served as evidence in police records and as a form of historical documentation. At the same time, however, its chemical process of mixing volatile substances and its capacity to reveal what would otherwise be invisible gave early photography a magical, even suspect quality. Photography and spirit photography were bound together by this same unpredictable process of development. The word “occult” carries the meaning of “hidden knowledge.” In this sense, occult photography sought to make visible an invisible, hidden world—the latent plasticity of the world and its hidden creativity.

It was this expectation—that photography possessed an automatism capable of revealing a hidden, surreal world, an automatic productive force independent of human agency—that drew the Surrealists, who placed automatism at the center of their methodology, so intensely to photography. The emergence of an image through chemical reactions in photography shares the same structure as a spirit medium, who similarly makes the invisible visible. Photography is thus the perfect medium, in both senses of the word. Through its chemical plasticity, photography binds together different worlds and reveals another, invisible nature.

In this way, photography transmits a hidden world into the here and now. For example, Sugiura’s The Kitten Papers (1992) was made by leaving two kittens alone in a darkroom for a week and turning the traces they left—their footprints and movements—into the work itself. The traces are made not by the artist but by cats moving of their own will; they record the cats’ unpredictable movements, which are beyond human intention. This device—a cat in a darkroom—recalls the thought experiment in quantum mechanics known as “Schrödinger’s cat”, in which a cat sealed inside a box is described as simultaneously alive and dead—an object in quantum superposition. Here the contents of the box constitute a literal “black box”, and whether the cat is alive or dead cannot be known until the box is opened.

Although Schrödinger’s cat is a thought experiment modeling the indeterminacy of measurement in quantum mechanics, Sugiura’s The Kitten Papers is an experiment actually carried out in a darkroom. Among the works exhibited in this exhibition, Story of Catfish , made by Sugiura during the same period, belongs to the same artistic trajectory. In both The Kitten Papers and Story of Catfish , the accumulation of uncontrollable, probabilistic deviations produced by the behavior of animals in the darkroom appears as material traces fixed onto photographic paper.

An important point to note is that the word “Papers” in The Kitten Papers evokes the documentary practice of reconstructing an event after the fact from its material traces—a movement of nature that no one observed. Here, Sugiura functions simultaneously as the maker and observer.

Sugiura’s photograms, in dealing with the physical movement of living creatures in the darkroom, reveal the countless deviations possible within nature—the superposition of multiple worlds. The unrestrained movement and energy of these creatures arise not because the world is fixed and static, but because countless possibilities remain latent and open within it. It is because these innumerable worlds are superimposed simultaneously, that the world possesses creativity. Here, the living creature is not merely an object being photographed, but it is itself the subject that produces the image.

The fact that Sugiura has repeatedly chosen living things—such as humans, animals, and flowers—as her subjects is congruous with her interest in the formation of natural forms. A living creature, which produces its own form through its own agency, is structurally similar to photography, which also produces an image automatically (for example, a flower grows by its own power and forms its own shape as a flower, entirely by its own power). As Sugiura herself has said, a flower is a reproductive organ: the stamen produces pollen, and the pistil receives that pollen to create a new life that ultimately becomes the seed.

Sugiura’s works that bind flowers together with thread appear to show, quite literally, the conjunction of male and female—pollination and fertilization—within a process of biological reproduction. Here, photography’s automatism responds to nature’s process of self-formation.

The photographic emulsion itself is, materially, a forced homogeneous dispersion and suspension of substances that do not naturally dissolve into one another—a mixture of water-based gelatin and fine particles of silver salts. The very support of a photograph embodies, at the material level, the conjunction between heterogeneous elements, as photography arises through an operation—emulsification—that binds together things that are chemically unmixable by nature. This operation recalls the Hindu creation myth of the Churning of the Ocean of Milk, in which every manner of plant and seed is placed into the ocean of milk and churned, and from that churning, the sun, the moon, the gods, and all animals are born.

This conjunction in reproduction and photography can also be linked to the alchemical term coniunctio . In the alchemical process, the chymical wedding—the chemical marriage of opposites, sulfur (the male principle) and mercury (the female principle)—was said to produce a new substance: the philosopher’s stone. Coniunctio meant a chemical conjunction, while at the same time serving as a metaphor for the conjunction of the sexes.

The mixing and blending of heterogeneous elements—emulsification—could be thought of as the emergence of life itself. The human body, living creatures, flowers, and the earth itself—subjects that Sugiura has persistently captured—belong precisely to this realm of nature and living things, onto which she superimposes the chemical process of photography’s own formation, together with her own acts of painting and image-making. Photography, rather than serving as a means of reproduction, can be understood as a self-generating movement that, through acts of conjunction, generates new forms—releasing a creative productive force inherent in the world itself. Sugiura’s work reveals the ubiquity of an automatic creative power that permeates the world.

Born in Japan and based in New York since 1967, Kunié Sugiura has spent more than six decades developing a body of work at the crossroads of photography, painting, and sculpture. Through a selection of works made over the past sixty years, Ubiquitous Conjunction looks back at a practice that has never ceased to push the boundaries of the photographic medium and to explore the possibilities of its dialogue with other art forms.

Ryo Sawayama

Curated by Ryo Sawayama

article_text:
La guerra come esperienza individuale e collettiva, ma anche come materia di riflessione critica, lontana dalle narrazioni ufficiali e dalle memorie costruite dalle comunità e dagli Stati. È da questa prospettiva che prende avvio una delle linee di ricerca della 19ª Biennale di Istanbul , in programma dal 18 settembre al 14 novembre 2027. Organizzata dalla Istanbul Foundation for Culture and Arts (İKSV) , istituzione culturale non profit attiva dal 1973, la prossima edizione vedrà Artİstanbul Feshane come sede principale, mentre gli altri spazi espositivi saranno comunicati successivamente. A curare la Biennale saranno l’artista e curatore Liu Ding e la storica dell’arte e curatrice Carol Yinghua Lu , che hanno aperto una call internazionale rivolta agli artisti provenienti dalla Turchia e dall’estero. L’invito riguarda in particolare chi sta vivendo o ha vissuto esperienze di guerra e desidera confrontarsi con questa realtà attraverso il proprio lavoro.

Le candidature potranno essere presentate online dal 19 ottobre al 22 novembre 2026, entro le 23:59, ora locale di Istanbul.

Questa diciannovesima edizione raccoglie un’eredità travagliata: la 18ª Biennale, inizialmente prevista per il 2024, era stata infatti rinviata al 2025 in seguito alle polemiche sulla nomina di Iwona Blazwick , scelta dall’İKSV nonostante il comitato consultivo avesse indicato un’altra curatrice, Defne Ayas . Le contestazioni avevano portato alle dimissioni di Blazwick e di diversi membri degli organi consultivi, con la successiva nomina di Christine Tohmé e con un progetto concepito come un percorso distribuito su tre anni. Il programma, tuttavia, è stato interrotto dopo la prima fase espositiva – conclusasi il 23 novembre 2025 – in seguito alle dimissioni della curatrice per motivi personali.

La guerra come campo di ricerca

Nel testo che accompagna la call , i curatori chiariscono che l’arte non può porre fine ai conflitti né risolverne le cause, ma può contribuire ad aprire spazi di dissenso, dubbio e immaginazione di alternative. «Guardare alla guerra attraverso l’arte comporta una responsabilità storica, oltre che un valore pratico, poiché permette di tenere a mente ciò che le narrazioni ufficiali omettono. Mettendo da parte – e talvolta contrapponendo – le testimonianze individuali alle memorie costruite da comunità e stati, gli artisti possono aprire la strada a prospettive più sfumate sulla vita in condizioni estreme e sulle questioni di coraggio, complicità, etica e resistenza che la guerra solleva».

Il tema della guerra, in ogni caso, non esaurirà l’interezza del programma della manifestazione, ma rappresenterà solo una specifica direttrice di ricerca all’interno di un quadro concettuale più ampio, che comprenderà ulteriori ambiti di indagine e che sarà annunciato nel dicembre 2026.

Come partecipare alla call

Le candidature sono aperte agli artisti di qualsiasi provenienza e disciplina. Per partecipare è necessario presentare una proposta di progetto che risponda direttamente ai temi indicati nel testo d’invito, per una lunghezza massima di 3.500 caratteri, spazi esclusi.

La domanda deve essere compilata online attraverso la piattaforma İKSV Slideroom e tutti i materiali devono essere caricati negli appositi campi del modulo e presentati in inglese o in turco. Gli artisti selezionati saranno invitati a partecipare a ulteriori conversazioni con i curatori, in presenza oppure online.

Il testo integrale dell’invito curatoriale e le informazioni sulla call sono disponibili sul sito ufficiale della Biennale di Istanbul .
